newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.N. says refugees die in Zaire, at least 200 drown.
newsitem.headline: U.N. says refugees die in Zaire, at least 200 drown.

text.p: The United Nations said on Friday that Rwandan Hutu refugees were dying in Zaire's jungles and drowning while crossing rivers, and it expressed alarm at their plight as the rainy season begins.

More than 100,000 hungry and exhausted refugees have arrived at the town of Ubundu on the Zaire River upstream from the eastern town of Kisangani after a long trek across the rainforest, fleeing advances by mainly Tutsi rebels fighting Zairean troops.

U.N. spokesman Fred Eckhard said 200 to 300 refugees drowned in a heavy storm in crossing the Zaire River in small boats on Thursday. One makeshift raft carrying 76 people was washed away and reports indicated the Rwandan refugees were paying as much as $2 a person to cross.

Some refugees were crossing the river in barges at the rate of about 800 per hour, leaving aid officials unable to cope with the large numbers. U.N. officials said about 7,000 had arrived by Friday morning.
The United Nations also appointed a new emergency Nairobi-based relief coordinator for the region, Pierce Gerety, an American, to succeed Martin Griffiths of Britain.

In Geneva, Chris Janowski, a spokesman for the U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR), said the rainy season would further complicate aid efforts in the remote rainforests of east Zaire, turn grass landing strips into mud and leave aid agencies with only one option to transport supplies across rivers -- by boat.
The refugees plunged deeper into Zaire with each rumoured rebel attack and aid agencies were following them with difficulty.
World Food Programme spokeswoman Christiane Berthiaume said a U.N. aid flight carrying food for refugees in Ubundu had to be cancelled on Friday because rains made landing impossible.
Janowski said that beyond Ubundu, "it is total wilderness. We'd have no logistics to help the refugees."

Janowski said some refugees were so weak they could not carry their small children and left them behind in the jungle. Typhoid, diarrhoea, skin diseases and malaria were the main health problems among those who had arrived.
"It was a harrowing journey. The refugees have had enough. They are in a terrible shape. There's been a trail of bodies left behind the refugees in the jungle," he told a briefing.
The refugees are hostage to Hutu militia and ex-soldiers who led 1994's genocide of minority Tutsis and cannot go back peacefully to Rwanda where a Tutsi-dominated army holds sway.

Many refugees killed or watched others kill during the slaughter of more than half a million Tutsis and Hutu moderates. The UNHCR failed to separate militia from the refugees at vast refugee camps in eastern Zaire and the world refused to send in troops to do the job, setting the stage for the current conflict.

The rebels said they were advancing toward eastern Zaire's military and regional hub Kisangani, defended by Zairean troops, foreign mercenaries and allied Rwandan Hutu militiamen. Janowski said Hutu militiamen were accompanying the refugees but that UNHCR had no evidence they were forcing them deeper into Zaire on a death march.

The United Nations believes there are still about 350,000 Rwanda refugees in Zaire, with about 200,000 Rwandan Hutus unaccounted for after they fled an earlier rebel advance on Tingi-Tingi, the UNHCR says.
